searchText: Has there historically been much discussion about allowing EOAs to deploy code at their address? The original AA proposal with the standard code. Which was supposed to be opened up to arbitrary code, in due time. original, like EIP-86? the one which was an issue, it is so old 🙂 ohhh okay, thanks 🙂 https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/issues/28 are there any technical concerns of doing something today off the top of your head, given EIP-3607? https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/718596092828057631/934091911424245771 My proposal is to actually do that, initially only have a standard code allowing a blocklist for 3074-authorisations. Ah gotcha. I was thinking about this in the context of also potentially being an alternative to 3074 because if a CREATE3 like op allowed an EOA to execute init code in its context, it sort of allows the same interface as 3074 except a little more costly to use since the code needs to be put into memory and the calldata needs to also be passed through another layer this also gives gives a 1 time revocation of all signed 3074 message, since once code is deployed it can't run init code not sure if that is along the lines of what you were thinking Since that weth3074 thing I can't get it out of my head to have a solution for weth. Just doing smart contract wallets and not something along the lines of 3074 doesn't make that possible, which made me think more positively about 3074 🙂 And doing authorisations vs. fully fledged EOA contracts is again a different level of risk. Maybe this is a wrong, as it is the same. Once a contract is authorised in the name of an EOA, it looks like a contract if executed via auth. the main diff in my mind is that it is a weaker risk assumption than a smart contract because it's possible the pk is possessed which can override an invoker
